diagnostic_evidence.quote: Wahba's problem aims at finding a nonzero quaternion $\qq$ that minimizes the cost function
an analytical expression for the solution set of $f(\qq)=0$ when $\ell=2$
has a solution if and only if $(\qa[1],\qa[2]) \sim (\qb[1], \qb[2])$
The presented results offer a complete theoretical characterisation of the Wahba problem in quaternions
thereby improving computational efficiency and analytical clarity of the solution

issues.failure_explanation: The paper defines Wahba's problem as minimizing f. It claims to solve it for l=2, to give a complete characterisation, and to improve efficiency over eigen-based methods. The formal results only describe the zero set of f. By the existence theorem, that set is nonempty only under exact pairwise similarity: equal real parts, equal norms and equal inner products, i.e. noise-free consistent data. For generic measured data the minimum is positive, and no minimizer is given. The efficiency comparison is therefore not like-for-like: Davenport, QUEST and the other cited methods solve the general minimization. No complexity analysis is provided.

failure_location.quote: In this paper, we solve the Wahba's problem for the special and practically important case $\ell = 2$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the introduction, abstract and conclusion claims to the zero-cost (pairwise-similar, noise-free) case. Remove the efficiency claim, or substantiate it with an analysis restricted to that case.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised scope (solution of Wahba's problem for l=2, complete characterisation, efficiency gain over eigen-methods) is not supported. Only the exact zero-residual case is covered.
issues.title: Claim to solve Wahba's (least-squares) problem for l=2 when only the zero-cost case is treated
issues.why_classification: The formal content is unaffected, but correcting the prose withdraws the advertised claim of solving the l=2 minimization problem. That is a material narrowing beyond a local wording fix.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Hence, $(\qa[1] + \qa[2]) \sim (\qb[1] + \qb[2])$, that is there exists a nonzero quaternion $\qq$ such that
Set $\qq = \qq[1]\qq[2]$, where $\qq[2]$ is a nonzero quaternion such that $\qb[1]\qq[2] = \qq[2]\qb[1]$.

issues.failure_explanation: In the converse, q in (SUM_SIMILARITY) is some quaternion mapping a1+a2 to b1+b2. Then q is redefined as q1q2 with q2 an arbitrary element commuting with b1, and the two are treated as the same q. Nothing shows that any q1q2 satisfies (SUM_SIMILARITY); existence of a single q doing both is exactly the claim to be proved. Read literally, the argument would show that every q with q^{-1}a1q=b1 maps a2 to b2, which is false. For example, take a1=b1=i, a2=b2=j, q1=1, q2=i: then q^{-1}jq=-j. Also, a1+a2 may be real (a2=-a1), where the similarity definition and characterization lemma do not apply. The statement is true, but its sufficiency direction is unproved.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the converse with a direct argument. After fixing q1, c=q1^{-1}a2q1 and b2 have equal real parts, equal imaginary norms and equal inner product with Im b1. So their components along Im b1 agree and their perpendicular components have equal norms. A quaternion q2 commuting with b1 (a rotation about Im b1, e.g. from the Sylvester solution formula applied to the perpendicular components, or 1 if they vanish) maps c to b2.
issues.overall_effect: The checkable necessary-and-sufficient condition (norms, real parts, Re(a1a2)) for zero Wahba cost is unproved in the 'if' direction. The existence theorem itself is only definitional, so contribution (i) loses its verifiable form.
issues.title: Sufficiency proof of pairwise-similarity characterization conflates two different quaternions q
issues.why_classification: The statement survives, but the sufficiency direction needs a genuinely new, though contained, argument rather than a local patch.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses allow Im a1 x Im a2 = 0 together with pairwise similarity, e.g. a1=i, a2=2i, b1=j, b2=2j. Then a3=b3=0 are real, so 'a3 ~ b3' and the cited Sylvester solution theorem (which requires similar nonreal quaternions) do not apply. The q2 formula takes the square root of 0, outside the square-root lemma; read as 0 it gives q=0, which is excluded. In this case the second equation is redundant and the true solution set is the entire family q1 of (Q1). The stated 'general solution' is therefore undefined or wrong.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a case split. If Im a1 x Im a2 = 0, pairwise similarity forces Im a2 = c Im a1 and Im b2 = c Im b1, so the general solution is q1 from (Q1) by the single-equation corollary. Otherwise assume Im a1 x Im a2 != 0 and keep the proof.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed complete closed-form solution set fails for collinear observation pairs.
issues.title: Main solution formula breaks down for parallel observations (a3=b3=0)
issues.why_classification: This is a degenerate-case fix using an already proved corollary. Method, conclusion and advertised scope survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $\qp$ is either an arbitrary pure quaternion if $\qa$ is a negative real

issues.failure_explanation: The step drops the lambda2 term, assuming sqrt(a3 b3^*) commutes with b1. When a3=-b3 (reached for every data set at one ratio lambda1:mu1), this square root is an arbitrary pure p, with p perpendicular to a3 by the side condition. Such p commutes with b1 only if p is parallel to Im b1. The statement also keys the condition on q1^*(..)q1 = |q1|^2 a3, which equals -b3 only if |q1|=1, so otherwise no constraint is imposed. Counterexample: a1=b1=i, a2=b2=j, lambda1=0, mu1=1/2 gives q1=i and q1^*kq1=-k. The condition allows q2=j, so q=k; but k^{-1}ik=-i and f(k)=8. With mu1=1 (q1=2i), no condition triggers and q2=k gives q=-2j, again not a solution.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the side condition in terms of a3=q1^{-1}(Im a1 x Im a2)q1. When a3=-b3, require q2 to be a nonzero real multiple of Im b1 (pure, perpendicular to a3 and commuting with b1); alternatively restrict q1 so that a3 != -b3. Then redo the commutation step with this case analysis.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed general solution set includes quaternions with nonzero Wahba cost, so the main closed-form characterization is false as stated.
issues.title: Antipodal case a3=-b3 mishandled: stated general solution contains non-solutions
issues.why_classification: The main theorem's statement must be corrected and a supplementary case argument added. The closed-form result survives in comparable form without new proof architecture.
